Another criterion is leverage. This measures the difference between observed and expected co-occurrences, focusing on actual impact and not just the ratio. Two rules can have the same lift, but one affects far more transactions, making it more useful.

Some researchers use 'leverage' = leverage(A,B) = s(A∪B) – s(A) x s(B), which measures how often A and B co-occur compared to if they were independent, differing from lift in that it uses an absolute ratio. Some also use 'conviction' = (1 – s(B))/(1 – c(A→B)), which measures how often the rule makes an incorrect prediction (high conviction means the rule is rarely wrong) and is sensitive to the direction of the rule.
